PROJECT LANTERN 7 STATUS REPORT
Community Library Appointment Pilot Program
Reporting Period: October 2026 - December 2026

---

ENTRY 1: October 3, 2026

Project Lantern 7 entered active development following approval of the scope document on September 28. The pilot targets three branch locations in the Metro District system: Central Branch, Riverside Annex, and the Highland Park satellite library. The core objective is to replace the existing paper sign-up sheet system with a digital appointment booking interface accessible via web and SMS.

Scope boundaries: The system will manage appointment slots for study rooms, meeting spaces, and one-on-one consultation sessions with library staff members. We are not handling circulation or checkout workflows in this iteration. The booking window is limited to 30 days ahead, and cancellations must be processed at least 4 hours before the scheduled time.

Team composition includes five developers (backend, frontend, database specialist), two QA engineers, and one product manager. The testing environment was provisioned on October 1 using replica data from the Central Branch's existing paper logs, converted to JSON format. Initial load testing showed the prototype could handle up to 150 concurrent booking requests without degradation, though response times increased from 200ms to 1100ms under peak load.

Acceptance criteria are documented in the project charter. All staff members at the three pilot branches have been notified of the upcoming change. We anticipate a soft launch on November 15, with a two-week parallel-run period where both digital and paper systems will operate simultaneously.

---

ENTRY 2: October 17, 2026

Functional testing of the core booking flow completed on October 15. Test scenarios included: new user registration, room availability verification, single and recurring appointment creation, email confirmation delivery, and calendar integration with the library's existing scheduling system. Of 47 test cases in the primary booking path, 44 passed on the first execution. Three cases required rework: one involved timezone handling for after-hours appointments, another revealed a race condition when two users attempted to book the same slot simultaneously, and the third exposed incorrect count calculations in the availability display after a cancellation.

All three issues have been remedied and re-tested successfully. The timezone fix involved adjusting the backend's UTC conversion logic to account for the Metro District's transition into daylight saving time boundaries. The race condition was resolved by implementing optimistic locking at the database layer using version counters. Availability count updates now flush to cache within 300 milliseconds of any state change.

Secondary testing focused on the SMS booking pathway, which allows patrons without email addresses to receive appointment confirmations via text message. Delivery tests were executed across three carriers (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) and all confirmations arrived within 45 seconds of booking. One carrier showed occasional 8-minute delays, but investigation attributed this to network congestion rather than a system defect.

Permission model testing was completed with realistic role matrices. Library staff members have distinct permissions for view-only, cancellation, and administrative functions. The permission layer was tested against 23 different role combinations without incident. No security vulnerabilities were identified in the October audit.

---

ENTRY 3: October 31, 2026

User acceptance testing (UAT) with real staff members from the Central Branch occurred on October 29 and 30. Twelve staff members participated in a 4-hour session where they performed booking, cancellation, and reporting workflows using the live test environment. Participants were given realistic patron requests and asked to complete end-to-end tasks. Satisfaction scores averaged 7.8 out of 10. Feedback was overwhelmingly positive regarding the speed and simplicity of the interface. Staff members appreciated the automated reminder emails, which they noted would reduce no-show rates.

Two minor usability issues emerged during UAT. The first involved the cancellation button placement: staff expected it to appear on the appointment list view, but in the current design it only appears after drilling into individual appointment details. This required an extra click and felt unintuitive. The second issue was that the system did not clearly communicate to staff whether a cancellation had succeeded or whether it had failed due to being within the 4-hour window. Users received neither a clear success confirmation nor an error message; the interface simply returned to the previous view.

Both issues are categorized as low-risk improvements rather than blocking defects. We plan to address them in a post-launch iteration. The 4-hour cancellation cutoff rule was confirmed to align with the library's existing operational requirements.

System performance during UAT remained stable. No timeouts or errors were recorded across 300+ simulated patron booking requests. Database query times averaged 145ms at the 95th percentile.

---

ENTRY 4: November 7, 2026

Pre-launch testing began on November 4. This phase validates the deployment pipeline, database migration scripts, and failover procedures. The database migration involved converting approximately 2,847 historical appointment records from the paper archives into digital format. This conversion was performed on a staging replica and cross-checked against scanned images of the original sign-up sheets. Spot-check verification confirmed 99.2% accuracy in the converted records. The remaining 0.8% variance was attributed to illegible handwriting in the source documents.

Disaster recovery testing was completed on November 5. We simulated a primary database failure and confirmed that the backup server assumed read-write responsibilities within 47 seconds. Appointment data was preserved without corruption. A second test simulated network partition between the application servers and the database layer. The system correctly returned error messages to users rather than attempting to write incomplete data. Recovery from network partition took 3 minutes and 22 seconds, which exceeds our target of 60 seconds. Root cause analysis identified a timeout configuration that was set too aggressively. This has been increased to 90 seconds, and the test will be re-run in the post-launch phase.

Load testing with synthetic data confirmed the system can sustain 200 concurrent bookings without unacceptable degradation. However, a concerning observation emerged during stress testing at 300 concurrent requests: response times spiked to 4.8 seconds, and the frontend began showing timeout errors after 35 seconds of sustained load. This scenario is well beyond what we expect during the soft launch, but we have documented it as a known limitation that would require infrastructure scaling if traffic grows substantially.

Deployment to the production environment is scheduled for November 14, the night before the planned soft launch.

---

ENTRY 5: November 12, 2026

During final pre-deployment validation on November 11, a critical gap in the cancellation flow was discovered. The issue emerged during regression testing of the cancellation workflow under edge-case conditions. Specifically: if a patron initiates a cancellation request fewer than 4 hours before the appointment, the system correctly rejects the request. However, the rejection was happening silently. Users received no notification that their cancellation attempt had failed. Instead, the appointment remained on their calendar, and they had no clear indication that the system had prevented the cancellation.

This gap has significant operational implications. A patron arriving 2 hours before their appointment might attempt to cancel via the web interface, see no error message, and leave. The library staff member would then hold the reserved space, waiting for a patron who had believed the appointment was cancelled. This could create both patron frustration and inefficient resource allocation for staff.

The root cause was traced to the frontend logic. The cancellation button was being disabled conditionally based on time-until-appointment calculations, but this calculation relied on client-side JavaScript date interpretation. On some browsers and devices, timezone offset calculations were off by one hour, causing the button to be incorrectly enabled or disabled. Additionally, even when the button was correctly disabled, the user interface did not provide explicit feedback about why the action was unavailable.

Remediation was completed on November 11 and re-tested on November 12. The solution involved moving all time-based logic to the backend, where UTC conversion is centralized and consistent. The frontend now displays a countdown timer and explicitly shows the cancellation deadline. When a patron attempts to cancel after the cutoff, they now receive a modal dialog explaining the 4-hour policy and showing the exact time at which cancellations become unavailable. The message is templated to account for timezone display preferences.

Re-testing with 34 edge-case scenarios across multiple timezones and devices confirms the fix is working correctly. No residual issues were identified. However, we note that this discovery validates the importance of comprehensive edge-case testing before launch. The soft launch timeline remains unchanged.

---

ENTRY 6: November 17, 2026

The system went live at 9:00 AM on November 15. The first day of the soft launch proceeded without incident. Booking volume was moderate, with 143 appointments created through the digital system on November 15 and 156 on November 16. Simultaneously, paper bookings continued at approximately 89 appointments per day across the three branch locations. This dual-pathway operation was intended and represents successful parallel operation.

User feedback during the first two days has been positive. Staff members reported that the digital interface reduced time spent managing appointments from an average of 3.2 minutes per booking to 1.8 minutes. This 44% efficiency gain aligns with our projections. No critical issues have been reported. One patron contacted Central Branch to ask whether they could cancel via SMS (they initially believed SMS was bidirectional), but the staff member successfully redirected them to the web interface.

Monitoring dashboards show system performance metrics are stable. Average response time is holding at 187ms. Database CPU usage peaks at 34% during midday hours. No alert thresholds have been exceeded. The first instance of the 4-hour cancellation cutoff policy being enforced occurred on November 15 at 2:43 PM. A patron attempted to cancel an appointment scheduled for 5:30 PM the same day. The system correctly rejected the request and displayed the new explanatory modal dialog. We have no indication of patron dissatisfaction with this outcome.

One minor issue emerged: the email confirmation template contained an error in the signature line, where the library's phone number was formatted as "555-1234-67" instead of "555-123-4567". This was corrected within 3 hours and does not affect any functionality. All new confirmations now display the correct phone number.

The soft launch is proceeding as planned.

---

ENTRY 7: November 24, 2026

Two weeks into the soft launch, parallel operation metrics are being analyzed. A total of 1,847 appointments were created through the digital system between November 15 and November 24. Paper-based bookings during the same period numbered 1,204, representing a 60-40 split in favor of the digital pathway. This split indicates strong user adoption and justifies the continued investment in the digital system.

Cancellation behavior has been tracked carefully given the discovered gap from November 12. Since the cutoff policy has been in effect, 127 cancellation requests have been received. Of these, 84 were processed successfully (66%), and 43 were rejected due to the 4-hour policy constraint (34%). Staff members report that patrons who received the explanatory modal dialog generally accepted the policy decision without complaint, though some expressed initial frustration. No refunds or exemptions have been requested.

System performance continues to be stable. Average response time remains at 186ms, with a 95th percentile of 318ms. No timeout errors have occurred. Database query performance has been monitored with database logging enabled on 10% of requests; no slow queries exceeding 500ms have been detected.

One limitation of our current monitoring became apparent during this period: we lack visibility into how many patrons attempted to cancel but were deterred by the explanatory modal and decided not to proceed. The system logs the modal display event, but we cannot distinguish between patrons who acknowledged the message and accepted the policy versus those who abandoned the attempt. We have recorded 78 modal display events but only 43 subsequent rejections, which suggests some patrons are closing the dialog without proceeding with cancellation. This is likely the desired outcome, but we lack quantitative confidence in user decision-making at this stage.

A decision point is approaching regarding whether to proceed to full rollout across the entire Metro District system or to extend the pilot phase.

---

ENTRY 8: November 29, 2026

Post-launch optimization work has begun. Database indexes were analyzed and a new composite index on (branch_id, appointment_date, status) was added on November 28. Replication of this index to the backup database completed successfully, and query performance improved by approximately 18% for common reporting queries. This optimization was proactive and not driven by any performance issue.

The remainder of November brought 847 additional digital bookings, bringing the two-week total to 2,694. This volume has validated our infrastructure capacity projections. Under normal usage, the system is consuming 22% of allocated database CPU capacity, leaving substantial headroom for growth.

One incident occurred on November 26 when a batch email job designed to send 24-hour appointment reminders entered an infinite retry loop, causing email delivery to some patrons to be delayed by 3 hours. Root cause was traced to a misconfigured retry policy in the message queue. The queue was set to retry failed sends indefinitely rather than respecting a maximum retry count. This issue was remedied by adjusting the queue configuration and has not recurred. All affected patrons eventually received their reminders. No operational impact resulted because the reminders, though delayed, still arrived before the appointment window.

Feedback collection is ongoing through optional surveys presented after booking completion. So far, 234 patrons have completed surveys, with an average satisfaction rating of 8.2 out of 10. Common praise centers on the speed of booking, the convenience of email confirmations, and the ability to book outside library hours. Common suggestions for improvement request additional appointment duration options and the ability to book further than 30 days in advance. These are noted as enhancement requests for post-launch consideration.

---

ENTRY 9: December 5, 2026

The soft launch period concluded on December 3. Decision gates established in the project charter required evaluation of three criteria before proceeding to full Metro District rollout: (1) zero critical defects, (2) system uptime of 99.5% or better, and (3) staff satisfaction score of 7.5 or higher.

All three gates have been met. No critical defects were reported or discovered during the two-week period. System uptime was 99.84%, exceeding the target. Staff satisfaction measured at 8.1 out of 10 across 28 survey responses from the three pilot branches.

However, a pending decision remains about timing for the next phase. The Captain must decide whether to proceed immediately with an internal trial involving additional branches within the Metro District system, or whether to postpone this decision pending the completion of a comprehensive user behavior analysis that could take an additional 3-4 weeks.

If the internal trial is postponed, we would maintain the current three-branch soft launch through December and January while the analysis team collects additional data. Deferring the trial would reduce short-term deployment complexity and allow us to gather more granular behavioral metrics about how patrons and staff interact with the system under varying seasonal demand conditions. However, postponement would also delay revenue recognition for the pilot project and push full system rollout to Q1 2027. The analysis work would focus on understanding the 78 modal display events mentioned in Entry 7 and whether the current 4-hour cancellation policy is operationally optimal or whether it should be adjusted to 3 hours or 6 hours based on actual staff workflow patterns.

Alternatively, proceeding with the internal trial immediately would expand the system to five additional branches beginning December 15. This approach would validate the system under higher load conditions and provide evidence of scalability more quickly. A decision is needed by December 8 to allow adequate staff training time.

---

ENTRY 10: December 5, 2026

This entry documents known limitations and supporting evidence from the two-week soft launch that inform the Captain's pending decision about trial timing.

Evidence Limitation 1: Modal Interaction Semantics. We recorded 78 instances of the cancellation-cutoff modal dialog being displayed to patrons. We observed 43 subsequent cancellation rejections. However, we do not have event logs that distinguish between patrons who read the explanation and chose not to cancel versus patrons who accidentally dismissed the dialog or navigated away. Our backend logs show dialog display but not user interaction with the dialog itself. If we proceed with the internal trial without addressing this limitation, we will lack behavioral data about whether the current 4-hour policy is being accepted by users or merely tolerated due to interface friction. Recommendation: If the trial is postponed, we should implement additional instrumentation to capture whether users click an acknowledgment button within the modal or abandon the attempt.

Evidence Limitation 2: Seasonal Demand Variance. The soft launch occurred during late fall, when library appointment demand is historically moderate. The three pilot branches show consistent booking patterns, but we lack visibility into whether the system will perform equally well during busy periods (January through March for study group bookings, summer for meeting room events). Load testing and stress testing were conducted with synthetic data. Actual user behavior during high-demand periods may differ. If the trial is postponed, we would gain this seasonal evidence through natural observation during December and January.

Evidence Limitation 3: Edge-Case Timezone Handling. Although the November 12 remediation fixed the identified timezone bug, testing was performed across only 12 timezone offset combinations. The Metro District system operates across three time zones (Eastern, Central, Mountain). Future expansion might reach Pacific and Alaska time zones. We have not stress-tested the backend UTC conversion logic against the complexity of transitional dates during daylight saving time shifts in years with non-standard transitions.

The system is operationally sound and ready for expanded deployment. The identified limitations are not blockers to trial expansion. However, they represent gaps in our confidence about long-term system behavior under conditions we have not yet observed in production.

END OF REPORT

First prototype build completed and deployed to staging environment on 2026-08-24. Initial testing focused on patron-facing booking flow, notification accuracy, and admin dashboard functionality. QA engineer Sarah Delgado executed forty-three test cases covering appointment creation, date/time selection validation, availability constraints, and confirmation email delivery. Results showed ninety-eight percent pass rate with two minor UI issues identified: calendar widget occasionally displayed incorrect month headers on mobile devices, and notification template formatting caused line breaks in Outlook email client. Both issues logged and developer assigned fixes on 2026-08-26. Librarian liaison from Harbor Ridge tested booking flow with five patron volunteers on 2026-08-28 and reported smooth experience with single observation that confirmation screen text should clarify whether SMS notifications would incur carrier charges. SMS provider integration confirmed working; sample messages delivered within forty-two seconds of booking completion. Backup and disaster recovery procedures tested; restore from full backup completed in eight minutes forty-three seconds. No critical issues identified; project cleared to proceed with expanded user acceptance testing phase.

---

## Entry 3: 2026-09-14 — User Acceptance Testing Phase

Expanded UAT commenced 2026-09-09 involving twelve volunteer patrons from community across age ranges and technical backgrounds, plus all librarian staff from three pilot locations totaling fifteen participants. Test scenarios included booking single appointments, scheduling multiple appointments in sequence, modifying existing appointments, and receiving notifications. Participants completed ninety-seven appointment booking tasks across two-week test window with ninety-five percent completion success rate. Two participants encountered issues with password reset flow after forgetting login credentials; both instances involved email delivery delay of thirty-seven minutes, attributed to email server queue saturation during peak testing hours. Librarian team tested admin dashboard functionality including appointment list filtering, patron contact capabilities, and room availability overrides. Dashboard performance showed slowdown during peak traffic simulation when system processed simultaneous lookups from all three branch locations; response times increased from 200 milliseconds to 890 milliseconds at peak load of forty concurrent users. Developer assigned ticket to optimize database queries and implement result caching. Notification delivery tested across forty-six appointments; email delivery achieved ninety-seven percent success rate with two messages bouncing due to invalid patron-provided email addresses. SMS delivery achieved one hundred percent success rate across thirty-one test messages. Overall UAT results indicated system readiness with identified performance optimization needed before production deployment. No showstopper issues encountered.

---

## Entry 4: 2026-09-28 — Discovery of Cancellation Flow Gap

Critical issue discovered during UAT extended testing phase on 2026-09-26 when librarian liaison Rachel Okafor attempted to cancel appointment scheduled for 2026-10-03 through patron self-service portal. Patron had booked two-hour research consultation appointment at Westfield Public on 2026-09-25 at 14:00. Okafor initiated cancellation, system displayed confirmation message "Cancellation submitted successfully," but no cancellation confirmation notification was sent to patron via email or SMS. Review of system logs revealed cancellation request was recorded in database, appointment status was correctly updated to cancelled, and notification task was created in queue. However, notification dispatch function failed silently without returning error code. Issue was reproducible across all three pilot locations; subsequent testing showed approximately thirty-two percent of cancellation attempts resulted in missing patron notifications, while appointment status correctly updated regardless of notification delivery success. Root cause investigation initiated. This gap directly impacts patron experience and creates liability if patron arrives for appointment believing it remains valid. Librarians at all three sites reported this represents significant operational risk as staff would spend time confirming cancellations by phone for patrons who never received system notification. Issue escalated to development lead. All further UAT testing of cancellation flow suspended pending root cause analysis and remediation.

---

## Entry 5: 2026-10-05 — Root Cause Analysis and Repair Planning

Root cause analysis completed 2026-10-04. Senior developer Marcus Chen performed code review of cancellation notification module and identified architectural flaw: notification dispatch function was calling external email service synchronously while SMS service was called asynchronously. When email service experienced latency or temporary failure, entire notification dispatch function would timeout after eight seconds without attempting SMS delivery or retry logic. Email service experienced five brief outages lasting two to eleven minutes each during UAT period, explaining high notification failure rate. System recorded no error logs because timeout occurred in background worker process not connected to user-facing request. Repair plan established: refactor notification dispatch to implement asynchronous queue for both email and SMS, add retry logic with exponential backoff for failed notifications, implement error logging with alerting for notification delivery failures, and add monitoring dashboard showing cancellation notification success rates. Estimated repair effort: forty hours of development time plus testing and deployment. Development commenced 2026-10-04; refactoring scheduled for completion by 2026-10-13 to allow two weeks testing and validation before internal trial launch date. Librarian liaisons briefed on issue and timeline; all parties agreed this represents blocking issue that must be resolved before production use. Product owner approved expedited timeline and additional resources if needed.

---

## Entry 6: 2026-10-14 — Implementation of Cancellation Flow Fix

Cancellation notification refactoring completed and deployed to staging environment 2026-10-13 evening. New architecture implements dual notification queue with separate workers for email and SMS dispatch, allowing either channel to fail independently without affecting the other. Email dispatch now attempts up to four retries with exponential backoff: first retry after thirty seconds, second after two minutes, third after eight minutes, fourth after thirty minutes. SMS dispatch implemented with two retries at similar intervals. All notifications now logged with unique tracking ID allowing full audit trail of delivery attempts. Error alerting configured to notify development team via Slack within two minutes of any notification delivery failure. Monitoring dashboard deployed showing real-time cancellation notification success metrics, broken down by branch location and notification channel. New code reviewed by two developers and one QA engineer; no issues identified. Deployment procedure completed successfully with zero data loss and full rollback capability verified. System tested with cancellation requests from all three pilot locations; forty-seven test cancellations processed with one hundred percent notification delivery success. Edge cases tested including patron cancellations at 23:55 on Friday, system timezone handling across DST boundary, and cancellation during peak library hours when other booking operations occur simultaneously. All scenarios passed validation. Implementation also identified secondary issue: cancellation confirmation screen text did not clearly explain notification delivery might take up to thirty minutes due to retry queue. UI text updated to set proper patron expectations for asynchronous notification delivery.

---

## Entry 7: 2026-10-27 — Regression Testing and Validation

Comprehensive regression testing executed 2026-10-21 through 2026-10-26 following cancellation flow repair to ensure no new issues introduced and all original functionality remains intact. QA team executed baseline test suite of one hundred forty-three test cases covering all appointment lifecycle scenarios: patron registration, appointment booking across different room types and time slots, appointment modification including date and time changes, cancellation through both patron portal and librarian admin interface, notification delivery across both email and SMS channels, and multi-site scenarios where patrons book at different branch locations. All one hundred forty-three test cases passed. Performance regression testing verified database query optimization deployed previously still achieved desired performance; query execution times averaging one hundred thirty-four milliseconds for appointment retrieval, consistent with baseline. Admin dashboard response time testing showed improved performance compared to previous measurement; peak load of forty concurrent users now achieved response times averaging five hundred twelve milliseconds, improvement of thirty-one percent from earlier measurement of eight hundred ninety milliseconds. Stress testing conducted with simulated load of one hundred concurrent users creating and modifying appointments; system remained stable with graceful degradation and no data corruption. Cancellation notification specifically stress-tested with one hundred forty simultaneous cancellation requests; all resulted in successful notifications within retry timeout window. Email service failure simulation conducted by temporarily disabling email provider credentials; system correctly fell back to SMS-only notifications and logged all failures appropriately. No regression issues identified. System stability and reliability assessed as meeting production readiness criteria.

---

## Entry 8: 2026-11-02 — Evidence Limitations and Trial Preparation

Comprehensive testing to date has validated core functionality across controlled staging environment; however, inherent limitations exist in test evidence before production deployment. UAT involved only twenty-seven volunteer participants compared to projected two thousand patrons across three branch locations during actual trial. Volunteer participants are self-selected and likely more technically proficient than general population; testing did not capture behavior of patrons with varying technical comfort levels or accessibility requirements. Testing did not include scenarios where patron attempts cancellation while simultaneously librarian attempts to modify same appointment, or other race conditions possible only under high concurrent load. Real-world patron notification delivery success will depend partly on patron-provided email addresses and phone numbers; testing used known valid contact information while some portion of actual patrons may have stale or incorrect contact data in system. SMS delivery times in staging environment averaged four to eight seconds; actual SMS delivery in production may vary due to cellular carrier network conditions outside system control. Librarian workflow integration tested with high-level observation but not through actual daily operations; potential inefficiencies or edge cases in admin dashboard may only become apparent during sustained use. Testing did not include extended capacity testing beyond one hundred concurrent users; actual peak load during school holidays or community events may exceed tested scenarios. Product owner and librarian liaisons have reviewed limitations and agree evidence sufficient to proceed with controlled internal trial limited to single branch location (Westfield Public) for two weeks with close monitoring and support staff present to manage any issues and collect qualitative feedback from actual patrons and librarians.

---

## Entry 9: 2026-11-05 — Pending Captain Decision on Internal Trial

Internal trial readiness assessment completed. System achieves all defined acceptance criteria: appointment booking workflow functions reliably, cancellation flow including notification delivery works correctly in testing, admin dashboard provides librarians with required management capabilities, and performance metrics meet acceptable thresholds. QA sign-off completed 2026-11-04 confirming system ready for limited production use under supervised conditions. Proposed internal trial scope: Westfield Public branch location only, fourteen consecutive calendar days from 2026-11-20 through 2026-12-03, limited initially to forty available appointment slots per day across all room types and consultation times. On-site support staff from development team assigned to Westfield Public for first three days of trial to provide immediate issue resolution and collect real-time feedback. Librarian team trained on system administration procedures 2026-11-03 through 2026-11-04; all staff completed training modules on appointment approval, cancellation processing, patron account support, and error escalation procedures. Monitoring dashboard access provided to product team and librarian liaisons for real-time visibility into appointment activity and notification delivery metrics. Data backup procedures verified and tested; daily backup scheduled with one-hour recovery window. Patron communication plan prepared explaining trial nature and providing clear support contacts for technical issues. Rollback procedure documented and tested; system can be fully disabled and reverted to phone-based scheduling within two hours if critical issues emerge. Captain approval required to initiate trial launch on 2026-11-20. Decision pending.

---

## Entry 10: 2026-11-05 — Trial Timeline and Postponement Implications

Trial timeline and postponement impact assessment completed. Current schedule targets trial launch 2026-11-20 to allow fourteen-day trial period through 2026-12-03, providing feedback data to inform rollout decision by 2026-12-10. This schedule also aligns with librarian staff availability during lower-traffic period after library programming concludes and before holiday closure period beginning 2026-12-24. If trial launch postponed to 2026-12-04 or later, trial period would extend into holiday closure period (2026-12-24 through 2027-01-06) when library operates on reduced hours and patron traffic historically decreases seventy-two percent compared to regular periods. Trial data collected during holiday period would not reflect typical appointment demand or librarian workflow, undermining feedback quality for rollout decision. Postponing trial to 2027-01-07 or later would delay rollout to remaining branch locations until spring 2027 at earliest, pushing full network implementation timeline from projected January 2027 to April 2027. Development team currently fully allocated to Project Lantern 8; postponement creates risk that team resources become committed to other priorities, reducing capacity for full rollout implementation and support. Librarian training conducted 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-04; additional training would be required if trial postponed beyond two weeks, adding cost and librarian time. Patron communication materials prepared and ready for distribution 2026-11-15; redesigning materials for later date incurs revision costs. Westfield Public facility reserved for on-site support staff presence 2026-11-20 through 2026-11-22; facility unavailable for other programming during this window with advance commitments made. Rescheduling facility requires coordination with branch manager and may impact library programming priorities. Recommendation to proceed with trial launch as scheduled 2026-11-20 to maintain momentum, capture high-quality feedback during optimal seasonal conditions, and keep full-network rollout on track for January 2027. Awaiting Captain decision.

PROJECT LANTERN 9 STATUS REPORT
Community Library Appointment Pilot
===============================================

ENTRY 1 - 2026-08-03
SCOPE AND KICKOFF

Project Lantern 9 was chartered to build and pilot a community appointment scheduling system for three public library branches in Metro North. The initiative addresses a stated need: patrons currently book consultation slots (tutoring, tech support, citizenship prep) via phone calls, email threads, and physical sign-up sheets. The pilot targets a web-based booking interface serving approximately 800 monthly appointment requests across Riverside, Cathedral Hill, and Lakeshore branches.

Functional scope includes: patron self-service booking with date-time selection; staff dashboard showing scheduled appointments by branch and service type; automated reminder emails to patrons two days before appointments; and a cancellation mechanism for both patrons and library staff. Out-of-scope: integration with the legacy staff scheduling system, payment processing, and multi-language support. The team consists of four engineers (Audrey Lo, Marcus Webb, Jenna Kirkland, Chen Rodriguez), one product manager (David Sorensen), one UX designer (Nia Patel), and one QA analyst (Bryn Hardwick).

The technical platform is a Node.js backend with a React frontend, PostgreSQL for transactional data, and SendGrid for email delivery. The team committed to code review standards: all changes require two approvals before merge, with one approval from either Lo or Webb. Database migrations must include rollback verification. The team established a biweekly demo cadence and weekly standups Monday through Thursday. Three environments were provisioned: development (localhost), staging (shared, reset daily), and production (live). Initial deployment timeline targets October 15 with a two-week operational pilot before evaluation. Expected burn rate: 18 engineer-weeks total.

First priorities: data model design and schema review, authentication and authorization scaffolding, patron booking form build-out, and email template drafting.

===============================================

ENTRY 2 - 2026-08-17
INITIAL TESTING AND SCHEMA VALIDATION

Backend development proceeded through sprint one. The team completed the PostgreSQL schema with seven core tables: patrons (id, name, email, phone, created_at, updated_at), branches (id, branch_name, address, phone, capacity_notes), services (id, service_name, estimated_duration_minutes, description), appointments (id, patron_id, service_id, branch_id, scheduled_start_time, scheduled_end_time, status, created_at, updated_at), appointment_history (id, appointment_id, old_status, new_status, changed_by, changed_at), email_log (id, patron_id, appointment_id, email_type, sent_at, delivery_status), and staff_roles (id, staff_name, email, branch_id, role, permissions).

Schema review by Audrey Lo and Marcus Webb identified one constraint issue: the original design allowed staff to book appointments on behalf of patrons, but the email_log table did not track whether a reminder was triggered by system automation or manual staff override. This was corrected by adding a trigger_source enum column with values 'system_scheduled' and 'staff_manual'. Rollback plan verified: dropping the column and recreating the trigger logic does not break existing foreign keys.

QA analyst Bryn Hardwick began unit testing of the Node.js database connection layer. Test suite includes: successful inserts into all seven tables with valid data, constraint validation (non-null checks, unique email on patrons table), date range validation for appointments (scheduled_start_time must be after current time and before 90 days out), and rollback behavior for constraint violations. Unit tests run in PostgreSQL 14 on a containerized staging environment. All 34 unit tests passed. Audrey Lo spotted a missing index on the appointments table (columns: branch_id, scheduled_start_time) that would slow staff dashboard queries. Index was added and performance tested with 10000 synthetic appointment records. Query time dropped from 1850ms to 62ms.

Frontend development began with patron booking form wireframes. Designer Nia Patel created low-fidelity mockups showing branch selection dropdown, service type selection, date picker (jQuery UI initially), time slot selection, and patron contact information fields. The team reviewed on August 14 and requested one revision: time slots should display in patron's local time zone, not UTC. Patel incorporated browser-based time zone detection using JavaScript's Intl API. This was flagged for later testing to ensure accuracy across daylight saving transitions.

===============================================

ENTRY 3 - 2026-08-31
USER ACCEPTANCE TESTING AND STAKEHOLDER FEEDBACK

Sprint two focused on frontend completion and integration testing. Chen Rodriguez built out the patron booking form in React, consuming API endpoints created by Jenna Kirkland. The form captures: branch selection (radio buttons), service type (dropdown), preferred date (date picker, with disabling of past dates and dates beyond 90 days), preferred time slot (five-minute increments, 9am to 5pm), patron name (text), email (text, regex validation), phone (text, format 555-555-5555 required). Form validation logic prevents submission until all required fields are populated and valid.

Bryn Hardwick built a test harness with 47 integration test cases covering: successful booking with all valid inputs, rejection of bookings outside 90-day window, rejection of times before 9am or after 5pm, rejection of malformed emails, rejection of phone numbers that do not match required format, duplicate booking prevention (same patron, same service, same time slot within 24 hours), and 41 additional cases. Of 47 tests, 46 passed. One test failed: a patron attempting to book an appointment on a date when all time slots were full. The system did not prevent booking but assigned an overbooked time slot. This was root-caused to missing capacity logic in the backend endpoint. Jenna Kirkland added capacity checking: services table now includes max_concurrent_appointments (default 1), and the booking endpoint counts active appointments at requested time slot and rejects if count equals max. Re-run of the overbooked test passed.

Product manager David Sorensen arranged a stakeholder meeting with branch managers from all three pilot locations: Riverside (branch manager Patricia Chen), Cathedral Hill (branch manager Robert Kowalski), and Lakeshore (branch manager Angela Torres). The team walked through a live demonstration of the booking flow on staging using synthetic data. Branch managers provided feedback:

- Patricia Chen: appreciated the simplicity of date-time selection but requested that staff see a weekly view of appointments, not just a list. This was added to scope for sprint three.
- Robert Kowalski: noted that staff sometimes need to cancel patron appointments in bulk (e.g., if a tutoring service must close for a day). Bulk cancellation was marked as out-of-scope for pilot, to be considered post-launch.
- Angela Torres: asked whether patrons receive confirmation of their booking. The team confirmed: a confirmation email is sent immediately upon booking. She also asked whether staff are notified of new bookings in real-time. The team responded that a digest email would be sent daily. Angela accepted this.

UX designer Nia Patel conducted a usability test with five patrons (recruited from Riverside branch waiting area). Participants were asked to book a mock appointment using the staging interface. Four of five completed the task without help and reported the interface was intuitive. One participant (age 73, first-time computer user) requested a phone number for manual booking, indicating the online form felt risky. This feedback was noted but did not change scope, as the phone booking path (via branch staff) remains available.

===============================================

ENTRY 4 - 2026-09-14
CANCELLATION FLOW GAP IDENTIFIED

Sprint three introduced the cancellation feature and exposed a critical gap in the system design. The team built both patron-initiated and staff-initiated cancellation flows. Patron cancellation: logged-in patron views their booked appointments and clicks "Cancel" on a future appointment. A confirmation dialog asks "Are you sure? You will not be able to rebook this slot." Upon confirmation, the appointment status changes from 'scheduled' to 'cancelled_by_patron', and a cancellation confirmation email is sent. Staff cancellation: staff member logs into the staff dashboard, views appointments for their branch, and clicks "Cancel" on any appointment. A modal asks for a cancellation reason (dropdown: staff_illness, service_unavailable, patron_no_show, other; if 'other', free-text required). Upon confirmation, the appointment status changes to 'cancelled_by_staff', and a cancellation notification email is sent to the patron.

During sprint three testing, Bryn Hardwick discovered an edge case: if a patron's cancellation email failed to send (network timeout, SendGrid API error), the appointment was still marked 'cancelled_by_patron', but the patron had no confirmation and might believe their appointment was active. The appointment_history table recorded the status change, but the email_log table showed delivery_status 'failed'. No retry mechanism existed. This was identified as a data consistency risk: patrons might show up to an appointment that staff have freed, expecting the cancellation to have been communicated.

Follow-up investigation: the team reviewed email_log entries for the first 200 test bookings and cancellations in staging. Of 200 cancellation emails, 3 failed due to invalid patron email addresses (typos in test data) and 1 failed due to a transient SendGrid timeout. The timeout case is realistic; the invalid email cases are less likely in production but highlight the risk. The broader issue: there was no mechanism for staff to see that a cancellation email had failed, and no automatic retry or fallback notification.

The team classified this as a high-priority gap. Product manager David Sorensen assessed impact: during the two-week pilot, even one failed cancellation email could result in a patron showing up for a cancelled appointment, creating friction with branch staff. The gap would need to be closed before production launch.

Audrey Lo and Marcus Webb reviewed the cancellation flow design in a 30-minute meeting with David and Bryn. The decision: implement a secondary notification path. If a cancellation email fails (max 3 retry attempts over 2 hours), a staff notification is triggered: "Cancellation notification failed for Patron [Name] appointment on [Date]. You may wish to call them at [Phone]." This keeps the burden on staff only if automated delivery fails. The feature was added to sprint four scope.

===============================================

ENTRY 5 - 2026-09-28
REPAIR IMPLEMENTATION AND VALIDATION LOGIC

Sprint four focused on building the email retry and fallback notification system. Jenna Kirkland implemented a SendGrid webhook handler: when SendGrid reports a bounce, permanent failure, or complaint event for a cancellation email, the backend marks that email_log record with delivery_status 'failed' and triggers a fallback notification. The fallback is an in-app notification to the staff member who owns the cancelled appointment (via the staff_roles table) plus an email to the branch manager.

The notification logic: on initial cancellation email send, the system creates an email_log record with delivery_status 'pending'. A background job (running every 10 minutes) checks for pending emails older than 15 minutes and attempts resend via SendGrid. After three failed attempts, the email_log record is marked 'failed_after_retries', and a fallback notification is queued. The fallback notification is an in-app alert (displayed on the staff dashboard) and an email to the branch manager. The staff member who initiated the cancellation also receives an email summary at the end of each day showing any failed cancellation notifications and which patrons should be called.

Test coverage for this flow: Bryn Hardwick wrote 12 new integration tests:
1. Successful cancellation email send (delivery_status 'sent')
2. Transient failure followed by successful retry on second attempt
3. Permanent failure (three retries exhausted, status 'failed_after_retries')
4. Fallback notification creation after permanent failure
5. Branch manager receives fallback email
6. Staff member receives end-of-day summary of failed notifications
7. Multiple failed cancellations in same day (summary aggregates)
8. Staff member logs in and sees in-app alert for failed cancellations
9. Staff member clicks "Call Patron" link in in-app alert, prepopulates phone number in a draft SMS (placeholder for future SMS capability)
10. Cancellation request made but email service is offline; system queues fallback
11. Email service recovers after queueing fallback; fallback is still sent as safety measure
12. Patron cancels appointment via patron-initiated flow; same retry-and-fallback logic applies

All 12 tests passed. Bryn also manually tested the flow by temporarily disabling SendGrid API access on staging to simulate an email service outage. Fallback notifications appeared as expected on the staff dashboard within 20 minutes. The end-of-day summary email was delivered to the branch manager within expected time window.

One issue during testing: the background job that processes pending emails ran every 10 minutes, which could delay fallback notification by up to 10 minutes plus 15 minutes of pending time (total up to 25 minutes). David Sorensen requested that this be faster for critical notifications. The team reduced the background job interval from 10 minutes to 2 minutes. This increases database query frequency but only during the pilot period with an expected maximum of 800 appointments per month (fewer than 30 concurrent pending email states). Performance was validated: the background job query ran in under 50ms even when checking 50 pending emails.

===============================================

ENTRY 6 - 2026-10-06
REGRESSION TESTING AND END-TO-END VALIDATION

With the cancellation flow repair integrated, the team conducted a full regression test suite to ensure no existing functionality was broken. Bryn Hardwick ran the complete test suite: all 47 original booking tests plus 12 new cancellation-retry tests plus 25 staff dashboard tests plus 18 reminder email tests plus 22 authorization and authentication tests, totaling 124 test cases. All passed.

Chen Rodriguez also performed manual end-to-end testing across all three environments. Test scenario: Patron A books a tutoring appointment for October 10 at 2pm at Cathedral Hill. System confirms booking received. Two days later, a reminder email is sent (automated). One day before appointment, Patron A logs in and clicks "Cancel." System requests confirmation. Patron A confirms. Appointment status changes to 'cancelled_by_patron', and a cancellation confirmation email is sent. SendGrid webhook confirms delivery. Staff member (Robert Kowalski, Cathedral Hill branch manager) logs into staff dashboard and sees the appointment now marked with 'cancelled' badge. The tutoring service capacity for October 10 at 2pm is now available to other patrons.

Variant test: same scenario, but the cancellation email fails to send. After two minutes (within the retry window), system attempts resend. Resend fails again. After three total attempts, system queues a fallback notification. Robert Kowalski logs into the staff dashboard and sees an in-app alert: "Cancellation notification for John Doe (tutoring, Oct 10 2pm) could not be delivered. You may wish to call 555-0147." Robert can click a button to auto-populate the patron's phone number into a draft call or SMS. By end of business day, Robert also receives a summary email listing all failed cancellation notifications for Cathedral Hill.

Both scenarios executed as designed. Performance metrics: booking form response time 150-200ms, staff dashboard load time 300-400ms with 50 appointments displayed, reminder email batch send (all reminders for a given day) completed in 2-3 seconds for staging data volume.

Marcus Webb reviewed the codebase for the cancellation-retry and fallback systems. Code review notes: three findings, all minor. (1) A comment in the email_log schema was outdated and removed. (2) A variable name `fallback_notify_data` could be more specific; renamed to `fallback_staff_notification_payload` for clarity. (3) A potential null-reference error in the fallback notification template was caught and protected with a defensive check. All three findings were addressed, and code was re-approved.

===============================================

ENTRY 7 - 2026-10-13
PILOT LAUNCH AND FIRST-WEEK METRICS

Project Lantern 9 entered production on October 15, launching at all three branches. The team deployed to production at 9am local time on October 15. Deployment process: code merge approved, database migration executed in production (with rollback plan verified), backend service restarted, frontend assets uploaded to CDN, staff and patron interfaces tested by Bryn Hardwick using production credentials.

First week metrics (October 15-22):
- 127 patrons successfully booked appointments (target was 150 for week one, actual was 85% of target)
- 8 cancellations initiated by patrons (6.3% cancellation rate)
- 3 cancellations initiated by staff (all due to staff_illness)
- 22 reminder emails sent without issue
- 0 cancellation emails failed

Email delivery for the week: 350 total emails (confirmations, reminders, cancellations, digest summaries), SendGrid reported 98.3% delivery rate (344 delivered, 6 bounced due to invalid patron email addresses). Those 6 bounces were from test data entered by staff; in production, patron email addresses are validated during signup.

Staff feedback from branch managers:
- Patricia Chen (Riverside): "Smooth launch. Staff got some calls from patrons who needed help using the online booking; we walked them through it. The in-app dashboard is clear." Patricia requested one feature: the ability to export appointment lists as CSV. This was marked as post-pilot enhancement.
- Robert Kowalski (Cathedral Hill): "No issues. The confirmation emails are being delivered reliably. I appreciate the daily digest email." Robert's branch had the lowest booking volume of the three.
- Angela Torres (Lakeshore): "Going well. One patron called to cancel but couldn't reach the online cancellation button; staff cancelled it for her. The staff cancellation flow worked smoothly; patron got a cancellation email immediately."

During the first week, Bryn Hardwick monitored production logs for errors. Errors observed: two 404 errors (patrons attempting to access invalid appointment IDs), three timeout errors on the reminder email batch process (resolved by adding database connection pooling). No data loss or corruption observed. Database backups ran daily without issue.

One operational gap emerged: patrons who book offline (via phone call to branch staff) are not yet in the system. Staff asked whether they could use the web interface to create appointments for phone-booked patrons. The team confirmed this is possible but requires staff to manually enter patron details (name, email, phone). This manual entry is error-prone. The team noted this as a post-pilot improvement: implement a staff-facing "create appointment on behalf of patron" flow with validation.

===============================================

ENTRY 8 - 2026-10-27
EVIDENCE LIMITATIONS AND DATA QUALITY CONSTRAINTS

As the pilot progressed through weeks two and three, the team identified evidence limitations affecting confidence in the system's reliability claims. Bryn Hardwick documented these in a detailed report:

First limitation: SendGrid webhook events (bounce, permanent failure, complaint) arrive asynchronously and are not guaranteed to arrive. The SendGrid documentation states that webhooks are delivered with a minimum of 100 retries over 24 hours if delivery fails, but there is a small possibility (estimated <0.1% by SendGrid) that a bounce event never arrives. This means a cancellation email that actually failed to deliver might never be marked as failed in the email_log table, and no fallback notification would be triggered. The team's retry-and-fallback system assumes webhooks arrive. If webhooks fail silently, the gap persists.

Second limitation: the staff end-of-day summary email that lists failed cancellation notifications is sent via SendGrid, using the same service that may have failed to deliver the original cancellation email. If the branch manager's email address is on a blocklist or has a failing mailbox, the summary email itself will fail to deliver. The team would not know the branch manager did not receive it. This is a second-order failure mode.

Third limitation: the pilot data volume (127 bookings, 11 cancellations over week one-two) is insufficient to validate reliability at production scale. At full scale, the library system might handle 800+ appointments per month across all branches. The test coverage assumes failure rates of 1-3 per 200 events, but actual failure rates at scale may differ. Production email services experience lower failure rates under normal circumstances but can experience rapid increases during outages.

Fourth limitation: the time zone detection feature (Nia Patel's browser-based Intl API implementation) was tested only in Bryn Hardwick's local time zone (America/New_York). The system has not been tested during daylight saving time transitions. In March 2027 and November 2027, patron time zones will shift. It is unknown whether the browser-based time detection will remain accurate after the transition, or whether patrons will see incorrect time slots.

Fifth limitation: the cancellation email template includes patron name, appointment date, time, branch, and service. The template was designed for English-speaking patrons. The pilot serves Riverside (diverse immigrant population), Cathedral Hill (university neighborhood), and Lakeshore (residential). No translation was done. Non-English-speaking patrons may not understand the cancellation notification. This is a scope limitation (translation is out-of-scope for the pilot) but represents a real usability gap.

Sixth limitation: staff user roles and permissions are stored in the staff_roles table with a permissions column (free text or enum). The design does not enforce role-based access control (RBAC) at the code level. A branch staff member should see only appointments for their branch, but this is implemented via filtering in the JavaScript frontend, not in the backend API. A malicious actor could inspect network traffic, modify branch IDs, and potentially view or modify appointments for other branches. The team decided to defer RBAC security hardening to post-pilot.

David Sorensen and Audrey Lo reviewed this limitations report. David acknowledged that the pilot is exploratory and these limitations are acceptable for the two-week evaluation window. However, David flagged the time zone concern as worth validating before production release. He requested that the team plan a test in a different time zone before final go-live (currently scheduled for early November). This was added to pre-release checklist.

ENTRY 9 - 2026-11-03

If the internal trial succeeds, Sorensen recommended moving to a four-week broader pilot at all three branches before final production release.

Audrey Lo and Marcus Webb assessed the engineering effort required to support the internal trial:
- No new feature development needed (all existing features are available)
- Must monitor email failure rates more closely; Jenna Kirkland will add instrumentation to track SendGrid API response codes and latencies
- Must test time zone behavior: Chen Rodriguez will create a test script that simulates bookings across five different time zones and validates slot availability is consistent
- Must implement the staff-created-appointment flow: estimated at 1.5 engineer-weeks (Jenna Kirkland volunteered to lead)

Bryn Hardwick noted that the existing test suite would need 8-10 additional test cases to cover the staff-created-appointment flow (patron created on behalf of scenario, staff validation, email to patron, etc.). This would take 2 days.

The team discussed risk: if the internal trial is approved and launched November 10, the team has five working days to implement the staff-created-appointment feature (November 5-9). Code review, testing, and deployment would need to fit in that window. Alternatively, the trial could launch with the existing features only (no staff-created-appointment flow) and defer that feature to trial week two. Audrey Lo recommended deferring: "The time-zone test and failure-rate monitoring are the critical unknowns. Staff-created-appointment is a nice-to-have and can wait."

Additional external pressure: the Riverside branch has already promoted the appointment system to patrons and staff in local social media; postponement would require public communication about the delay. David flagged this as a communication risk but said he would handle external messaging if needed.

Captain decision needed: approval to proceed with internal trial on November 10, with the scope and risks described above.

ENTRY 10 - 2026-11-05
PENDING CAPTAIN APPROVAL AND TRIAL CONSEQUENCES

Summary of decision point: Project Lantern 9 has completed a two-week community library pilot across three branches. The system handled 387 bookings with 4.7% patron-initiated cancellation rate and 0.9% email failure rate. All three branch managers reported positive feedback. The team is now at a fork:

Path A (Recommended): Proceed with a two-week internal trial at Riverside branch starting November 10. Scope: monitor email delivery failure rates under slightly higher scale, validate time zone behavior before daylight saving time transitions, and gather stakeholder confidence. This path requires engineering to focus on monitoring and instrumentation (low effort, 2-3 days). If trial succeeds, the team moves to a four-week broader pilot before production release. Key unknowns still pending for the trial:
1. Email delivery failure rate at 500+ bookings (current pilot: 387 bookings, 4 failures). At higher volume, rates may increase if there is a latency issue or concurrency limit in the email sending code. The monitoring instrumentation will capture this.
2. Time zone accuracy during late-fall period. Current pilot happened in October (no transition date yet). 3. Staff and patron confidence. The pilot generated 12 user support calls and 2 minor bug reports. Trial will reveal whether support volume scales linearly or increases faster as users become more familiar with the system.

Consequences of proceeding: engineering resources allocated to the trial (Jenna Kirkland and Bryn Hardwick primarily) are not available for other work during November 10-24. The team accepted this trade-off. No other projects are currently in-flight.

Consequences of postponing: the two-week window (November 10-24) is freed. Engineering recommendation: proceed with trial. The unknowns (email failure rates at higher scale, time zone stability) are worth gathering before production release. The two-week delay is acceptable and buys important evidence.

PROJECT LANTERN 10 - STATUS REPORT SERIES
Community Library Appointment Scheduling Pilot
Fictional Project Documentation

================================================================================
ENTRY 1 - 2026-09-03
Report Period: August 25 - September 2, 2026
Status: On Track

Project Lantern 10 launched its initial phase on August 25 with a focused scope: develop and test a web-based appointment scheduling system for three fictional library branches in the Greenbrook Metro system. The pilot targets library patrons seeking in-person reference consultations with trained staff members. The three participating branches are Central Greenbrook (65 staff slots per week), Riverside Branch (42 slots), and North End Library (38 slots), totaling 145 weekly available appointment windows.

The core technical scope includes a patron-facing booking interface, a staff-side view for appointment confirmation and notes, cancellation and rescheduling capabilities, notification delivery via email, and administrator dashboards for utilization reporting. The system runs on fictional technology: a Django 4.2 backend connected to PostgreSQL 15, with a React 18 frontend hosted through Vercel. Authentication uses OAuth 2.0 integration with the existing Greenbrook Library System identity provider.

Early testing commenced with unit test coverage across appointment creation, availability checking, and email notification generation. The backend achieved 84% code coverage on critical paths after initial test writing. The frontend passed basic interaction tests for the booking calendar view, form submission validation, and error state handling. No critical blockers identified in the first week.

Stakeholder alignment confirmed with library directors from all three branches on August 30. They confirmed current waiting list lengths: Central Greenbrook averages 18 pending requests, Riverside has 12, North End has 8. Directors estimated that 60 percent of cancellations occur with less than 48 hours notice currently. The pilot aims to reduce last-minute gaps through automated cancellation handling.

Technical team members assigned: backend development led by Marcus Chen, frontend development led by Sarah Okonkwo, QA and testing led by James Morrison, and project coordination by Patricia Valencia. First integration testing scheduled to begin September 5. No resource constraints anticipated at this stage. All team members have library systems domain experience from prior projects.

================================================================================
ENTRY 2 - 2026-09-10
Report Period: September 3 - September 9, 2026
Status: On Track

Integration testing commenced as scheduled on September 5 with a focus on end-to-end flows from patron login through appointment confirmation. The complete user journey for booking a new appointment was tested across all three branches simultaneously. Test data included 240 mock patron accounts and 480 pre-created appointment slots distributed across the three weeks of testing.

The appointment creation flow validated successfully. Patrons logged in using test OAuth credentials, viewed available time slots by branch preference, selected a 45-minute window, and received confirmation emails within 2 minutes of booking. Email delivery reliability measured at 98.4 percent on 234 test bookings. Three confirmations failed due to fictional email gateway throttling, which was expected in the test environment. The backend recorded all bookings in PostgreSQL with timestamps, patron identifiers, and staff assignments.

Staff-side confirmation interface testing revealed minor UI inconsistencies. Staff members viewed their assigned appointments in a daily and weekly view. The weekly view displayed correctly, showing all 145 slots across three branches with patron names, contact information, and reference request summaries. The daily view showed only 18 of 24 expected appointments on September 6. Investigation identified a timezone conversion bug: the daily view was retrieving appointments in UTC while displaying times in Eastern Time without proper offset calculation. Marcus Chen deployed a patch on September 7 that corrected the timezone handling. Retesting on September 8 confirmed the daily view now displays all scheduled appointments.

Email notification content testing passed for both patron and staff messages. Patrons received appointment confirmation with date, time, location, and cancellation instructions. Staff members received advance notices 24 hours before scheduled appointments. No formatting errors or missing information detected across 156 test email messages reviewed.

Administrator dashboard reporting was tested with synthetic utilization data. The dashboard displayed appointment fill rates by branch, cancellation rates by day of week, and no-show tracking (a feature enabled by staff marking attendance after appointments). Initial reports generated correctly on September 8. Dashboard load times measured at 340 milliseconds for weekly utilization views, well within the 1000-millisecond performance target.

Known issue: cancellation flow testing incomplete. The team began testing patron-initiated cancellations on September 9 but encountered workflow gaps that require further investigation. The testing showed that when a patron cancels an appointment, the system correctly records the cancellation timestamp and marks the slot as available. However, the process for reassigning the freed time slot and notifying the patron of the cancellation completion lacks clarity. James Morrison documented the gap and flagged it for priority review in the next testing cycle.

No other blockers identified. Team velocity on track with implementation phase. Remaining work: finalize cancellation flow, complete rescheduling logic, validate notification escalation for confirmed appointments with attendance tracking, and conduct user acceptance testing with actual library staff.

================================================================================
ENTRY 3 - 2026-09-17
Report Period: September 10 - September 16, 2026
Status: Blocked - Cancellation Flow Gap

The cancellation flow gap identified on September 9 expanded significantly during testing on September 10-13. Detailed investigation revealed multiple unhandled scenarios within the cancellation and rescheduling workflow that differ from initial requirements.

The discovered gaps are as follows: When a patron initiates cancellation through the web interface, the system generates a cancellation request record, records the timestamp, and marks the slot as available. However, staff members were not notified of the cancellation automatically. This is critical because staff at Greenbrook branches currently rely on confirmation calls one day before appointments; without cancellation notification, staff could prepare materials for appointments that no longer exist. A patron cancellation at 10:30 AM would result in staff discovering the gap only when the patron fails to arrive at the scheduled time.

Second gap: when a patron clicks the cancellation confirmation button, the system asks whether the patron wants to be offered alternative appointment times. If the patron selects yes, the system must gather new preference information (preferred date range, time of day, branch preference, and reason for rescheduling). The current interface collected this data in the confirmation dialog but did not persist it for later matching. The system would acknowledge the patron's preference without actually scheduling a follow-up or notifying the scheduler to prioritize that patron.

Third gap: cancellation reasons were not being captured. Library directors indicated on September 12 that understanding why patrons cancel is important for service improvement. The current cancellation form did not include a reason dropdown or text field. Patricia Valencia flagged this as a design requirement that was omitted during initial scoping.

Fourth gap: the system lacked a confirmation message showing patrons that cancellation had completed successfully. Patrons clicked the cancellation button, and the form submitted, but no success state message appeared. Testers could not confirm whether the cancellation was processed or the transaction had failed. This is a user experience failure that could lead to duplicate cancellation attempts or patron confusion.

Testing volume on cancellation scenarios was limited. James Morrison executed 34 manual cancellation tests: 18 for successful cancellations with no rescheduling request, 16 for cancellations with rescheduling preference indicated. Of the 18 successful cancellations, 3 failed silently (no success message), and the appointment was still marked as booked in the staff view despite the cancellation record existing in the database.

On September 13, Patricia Valencia scheduled a working session with Marcus Chen and Sarah Okonkwo to inventory all cancellation requirements and map the missing workflow states. The team documented five distinct cancellation scenarios that the system must handle:
1. Patron cancels, prefers no rescheduling, wants no further contact.
2. Patron cancels, wants to be rescheduled to a future appointment at library discretion.
3. Patron cancels, wants to remain on waiting list for specific future dates.
4. Patron cancels via phone through staff (staff-initiated on behalf of patron for no-show management).
5. System-initiated cancellation due to manual staff cancellation of appointment blocks (branch closed due to weather, staff illness, etc.).

The current implementation handles only scenario 1 partially. Scenarios 2-5 are either unimplemented or partially implemented with missing state transitions. This is a moderate scope increase but critical to the pilot's success.

Status escalated to blocked because cancellation flow repairs cannot be deferred to post-launch. Library directors confirmed on September 14 that cancellation is the single highest-traffic flow in their current system: of 145 weekly appointments, approximately 38 (26 percent) are cancelled or rescheduled weekly. Without correct cancellation handling, the pilot will increase staff burden rather than reduce it.

Repair plan initiated by Marcus Chen: redesign the cancellation API to support all five scenarios, redesign the patron-facing cancellation form with reason collection and success messaging, implement queue-based rescheduling for scenarios 2 and 3, and add staff notification for all patron cancellations. Estimated implementation time: 4 working days. Testing will require additional test cases for each scenario. No team member availability constraints; all three developers remain assigned.

Anticipated completion of cancellation flow repair: September 20. This will bring the overall project timeline to a one-week delay from the original September 15 go-live target.

================================================================================
ENTRY 4 - 2026-09-21
Report Period: September 17 - September 20, 2026
Status: Cancellation Flow Repair Complete - Testing Phase

Marcus Chen completed the cancellation flow redesign and implementation on schedule on September 20, one day ahead of the September 21 target. The implementation addressed all five cancellation scenarios identified in the previous report.

The redesigned cancellation API now distinguishes between patron-initiated and staff-initiated requests. Patron-initiated cancellations include a reason field (dropdown options: illness, schedule conflict, found alternative resource, other, prefer not to say) and a follow-up preference field (no rescheduling, rescheduled at discretion, keep on waiting list, contact later). The API validates that all required fields are provided before processing the cancellation request. Validation tests confirmed that missing reason or preference data triggers appropriate error responses on September 20.

Sarah Okonkwo updated the patron-facing cancellation form to include a success state. Patrons now see a confirmation message: "Your appointment has been cancelled. You may book a new appointment at any time." A cancel button also appears, allowing patrons to navigate back to the main booking interface. Form submission now includes explicit success and error feedback via modal dialog. Five different error states were tested: network failure, database write failure, email delivery failure, invalid appointment ID, and user authentication expiration during form submission.

The rescheduling queue system was implemented to handle cancellations where patrons request staff-discretionary rescheduling. When a patron cancels and selects "rescheduled at discretion," the cancellation is recorded with a flag in the database, and a scheduler notification is generated. Patricia Valencia reviewed the notification content on September 19. Scheduler notifications include patron name, reason for cancellation, preferred date range (if specified), and a link to view the patron's availability preferences. Notifications are routed to a fictional email address: greenbrook-schedulers@greenbrook.lib.

Staff-initiated cancellations were implemented to allow library staff to cancel appointments on behalf of patrons (for no-show management or branch closures). Staff access this through a separate admin panel with a dropdown to select the appointment to cancel and a reason field. The reason options for staff include: patron no-show, system closure, staff illness, facility issue, or patron request received via phone. Initial testing of the staff cancellation interface confirmed that all staff-initiated cancellations generate patron notifications (via email) within 5 minutes of the cancellation action.

Testing Phase Results (September 21-20): James Morrison executed 87 cancellation test cases across all five scenarios. Results: Scenario 1 (cancel, no rescheduling): 18 tests, 18 passed. Scenario 2 (cancel, staff-discretionary rescheduling): 19 tests, 18 passed, 1 failed due to email delivery timeout. Scenario 3 (cancel, remain on waiting list): 16 tests, 15 passed, 1 failed due to missing waiting list status update in the database. Scenario 4 (staff-initiated cancellation): 18 tests, 17 passed, 1 failed due to missing patron notification for a specific timezone edge case. Scenario 5 (system-initiated block cancellation): 16 tests, 15 passed, 1 failed due to incomplete cascade deletion of dependent appointments.

Total pass rate: 83 of 87 tests (95.4 percent). One test failure (waiting list status update) affects data integrity and requires priority remediation. Three test failures (email timeout, timezone notification, cascade deletion) are edge cases that should be handled but may not affect the core pilot functionality. Marcus Chen estimated 4 hours to fix the waiting list status bug and 2 hours per remaining failure for comprehensive edge case handling.

Evidence limitations: The testing environment does not fully simulate the actual load that the system will experience during pilot launch. No load testing was conducted on the cancellation flow with more than 50 concurrent cancellation requests. The team does not have data on whether the email delivery timeout observed in one test represents a systematic issue or an isolated network fluctuation. Database cascade deletion logic was tested with synthetic data but not validated against production schema complexity.

The team's confidence in the cancellation flow implementation is high for the primary scenarios (1-3), moderate for scenario 4 (staff-initiated), and lower for scenario 5 (system-initiated block cancellations). Recommendation from James Morrison: proceed with user acceptance testing for scenarios 1-3, defer scenario 5 to post-launch optimization, and treat scenario 4 as requires-caution until the timezone edge case is fully resolved.

Next Phase: User Acceptance Testing with actual library staff scheduled for September 24-26. Cancellation flow will be primary focus during UAT sessions. Team availability remains full; no resource constraints.

Status: UAT Complete - Minor Issues, Ready for Internal Trial Decision

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) conducted September 24-26 with library staff from all three branches. Participants: 4 staff members from Central Greenbrook, 3 from Riverside, 2 from North End, totaling 9 library staff members. Testing duration: 6 hours per branch (18 hours total), conducted in actual library environments with live network connectivity.

UAT focus areas: patron booking flow, staff confirmation interface, cancellation workflow, and rescheduling process. Results summary: Patron booking flow validated successfully. Staff confirmed that the interface matched their mental model of how the booking system should work. Cancellation workflow tested with 12 cancellation scenarios conducted by staff. All 12 cancellations processed successfully. Sarah Okonkwo estimated 1 hour to implement and test.

Estimated effort: 3 hours for implementation and testing. Decision deferred to post-launch phase.

Testing confidence: Library staff confirmed through exit interviews that the system handles their core workflow correctly. The cancellation flow, validated as the highest-priority gap two weeks prior, is now functioning reliably in a realistic library setting. No critical blockers remain.

Evidence limitations: UAT was conducted with staff members in a controlled setting, not during actual patron appointments. No measurement of how patrons will actually interact with the system under real conditions. The system was tested with synthetic patron data, not real patron accounts or behaviors. Three of nine staff members had prior technology experience above the library median; their feedback may not represent all staff skill levels.

Team Status: All team members remain assigned. No resource constraints. Working tree prepared for internal trial launch. Code is staged and ready for deployment to trial environment on a fictional trial server infrastructure.

The internal trial will run the system with real patron appointments at one branch (Central Greenbrook) for a two-week period. If the trial is approved, projected launch is October 1. Week 2-3 (October 8-14): Continued live appointments, data collection on appointment patterns and cancellations, staff feedback collection, system observation. If trial is postponed for more than two weeks, the team recommends a second round of UAT with fresh staff participants to validate that the system remains correct after any team context switches. Estimated cost of two-week postponement: 2-3 additional days of preparation work when the trial resumes. Cost of one-month postponement: full UAT re-run recommended, estimated 5 additional days of work. System code remains valid for at least 30 days without dependency updates or environmental changes.

Team Recommendation: Proceed with internal trial. The system is functionally complete for the pilot scope, validated by library staff, and ready for real-world testing. Deferral risks lack of momentum and requires repeat validation work.
